newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador vice president appointed as crisis ebbs.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador vice president appointed as crisis ebbs.

text.p: Ecuador's Vice President Rosalia Arteaga on Sunday was appointed head of a caretaker government that brought an end to the political crisis sparked by the ouster of flamboyant leader Abdala Bucaram.

Bucaram, dubbed "El Loco" -- "madman" -- for his sometimes bizarre behaviour, stepped down early on Sunday just six months after he won office, driven out by a paralysing strike and a revolt in the Congress.

A smiling Arteaga, a 40-year-old lawyer and former education minister, gave a brief speech at the ornate Carandelet presidential place, saying Ecuador "fortunately found a constitutional solution" to a crisis that had put it "on the edge of the abyss."
Acknowledging she would head a brief transitional government, she later told a news conference that "order has been restored ... the country is not paralysed ... we can guarantee security."
Legislators said Congress would meet on Tuesday to pass legislation allowing it to reappoint its leader, Fabian Alarcon, as president, with Arteaga returning to the vice-presidency.

Alarcon, 50, would in turn serve as interim head of state until Aug. 10, 1998, then hand over power to a new president chosen in general elections to be held in May or June next year, a vote the ousted Bucaram vowed to play a role in.
Arteaga's appointment resulted from late-night talks between legislators and military leaders who, political sources said, were reluctant to back any deal that had no legal standing.
In a joint statement on Sunday, the armed forces and national police reiterated "unyielding democratic vocation and absolute respect for the Constitution."
Alarcon was initially voted in as president by Congress on Thursday after two days of demonstrations protesting Bucaram's austerity plan led to the dismissal of Bucaram for "metal incompetence."
With a Constitution vague on the issue of succession, three people, Bucaram, Arteaga and Alarcon, all claimed the presidency, and leading legislators turned to the armed forces as the final arbiter.
Bucaram left the capital late on Friday and finally gave up his fight to save his presidency on Sunday, saying a military-backed "congressional coup" left him without power to rule.
He remained defiant, however, and said he was not dead politically in the Andean nation of 12 million people. Analysts agreed with his assessment.

"Bucaram is not finished, he'll continue to play an important role in politics. In the next elections people will seek to elect an outsider and that could well be Bucaram again," said Jaime Duran, head of polling and consulting firm Informe Confidencial.

In a rambling interview on national television granted at his home in the Pacific coast city of Guayaquil, Bucaram vowed to make a political comeback, saying: "I'm going to be a candidate for the presidency in the next elections."
And the man who campaigned last year as a champion of the poor yet enraged his impoverished nation with economic belt-tightening measures said Ecuadoreans would bitterly regret his dismissal.
"If you think I'm crazy today just wait to see what kind of craziness is coming in the future," he said.
In his traditional abrasive style, he said that if Alarcon was a man he would accept to meet him face-to-face. Alarcon curtly replied that duels were anachronistic.
Bucaram's popularity slumped sharply after the austerity measures, which included sharp increases in electricity, gas and public transport rates. The public apparently tired of his behaviour as well.

His antics included shaving off his moustache live on television and releasing a rock 'n' roll CD entitled "A Madman in Love." Tirades against political opponents and allegations of corruption and nepotism enraged an urban political elite to which Bucaram referred on Sunday as "plotting oligarchs."

"This is a national disgrace and what we've seen here is a coup," he said, adding that he would go to the United Nations, to the Organisation of American States and even to the Vatican to prove his point, "with the Constitution in hand."
